# Overview

**Purpose:** Understand how SEM connects regression, path analysis and CFA using `lavaan` in R.

- SEM allows multiple relationships to be tested together, including relationships between latent constructs.
- CFA focuses on measurement; SEM adds structural relationships.
- The main idea is to compare the observed covariance matrix with the covariance matrix implied by the model.

# Data Preparation

The UCLA example uses 500 students and nine observed variables.

| Construct | Indicators |
|---|---|
| Adjustment | motiv, harm, stabi |
| Risk | ppsych, ses, verbal |
| Achievement | read, arith, spell |

```{r}
#| label: packages
# install.packages("lavaan", dependencies = TRUE)   # run once
library(lavaan)
# Compact output for each model
brief <- function(fit) {
  p <- standardizedSolution(fit)
  print(p[p$op %in% c("~", "=~", ":="),
          c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est.std", "pvalue")], row.names = FALSE)
  print(round(fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")), 3))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: import
# Read the worland5 data straight from the UCLA site
dat <- read.csv(
  "https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/worland5.csv"
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Output: Examine
```{r}
#| label: examine
str(dat)        # 500 rows, 9 numeric variables
head(dat)       # first six students
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Output: Covariance
```{r}
#| label: covariance
# Sample covariance matrix S
round(cov(dat), 2)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Output: Correlation
```{r}
#| label: correlation
# Correlations are easier to read; with variances of 100 they are just S / 100
round(cor(dat), 2)
```
:::

**Notes:** The variables are centered, with sample variances of 100. Reading, arithmetic and spelling are strongly correlated.

| Matrix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Σ | True population covariance matrix |
| S | Sample covariance matrix from `cov(dat)` (divides by n − 1) |
| Σ(θ) | Covariance matrix implied by the model |

# SEM Concepts

| Term | Meaning / Example |
|---|---|
| Observed variable | Directly measured, e.g., `motiv` |
| Latent variable / factor | Unobserved construct, e.g., `adjust` |
| Indicator | Observed measure of a factor |
| Exogenous | Not predicted within the model, e.g., `risk` |
| Endogenous | Predicted by other variables, e.g., `achieve` |
| Loading | Relationship between a factor and its indicator |
| Regression path | Directional relationship between variables |
| Measurement model | Defines how factors are measured |
| Structural model | Defines relationships among constructs |
| Residual | Unexplained portion of a variable |
| Intercept | Expected outcome when predictors are zero |
| Covariance | Non-directional relationship |

**Path diagrams:** Squares = observed variables; circles = latent factors; single arrows = regressions or loadings; double arrows = covariances or variances.

## Matrix notation

$$
\eta = \alpha + B\eta + \Gamma\xi + \zeta
$$

- **Γ:** paths from exogenous to endogenous variables.
- **B:** paths among endogenous variables.
- **Λ:** factor loadings; **Φ:** exogenous covariance; **Ψ:** structural residual covariance; **Θ:** indicator residual covariance.
- ξ = exogenous factor, η = endogenous factor, ζ = structural residual.

# lavaan Syntax

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `~` | Regression | `read ~ motiv` |
| `=~` | Measurement | `adjust =~ motiv + harm + stabi` |
| `~~` | Variance or covariance | `motiv ~~ harm` |
| `~1` | Intercept / mean | `read ~ 1` |
| `1*` | Fix parameter | `f =~ 1*q01` |
| `NA*` | Free parameter | `f =~ NA*q01` |
| `a*` | Label parameter | `f =~ a*q01` |

The first loading is usually fixed to 1 to set the factor scale. `:=` defines a new parameter, such as an indirect effect.

# Regression and Path Analysis

## Simple regression

```{r}
#| label: m1a-lm
# Least-squares regression for comparison
fit_lm <- lm(read ~ motiv, data = dat)
coef(summary(fit_lm))
sigma(fit_lm)^2
```

```{r}
#| label: m1b-lavaan
m1 <- '
  read ~ 1 + motiv    # intercept (alpha) and slope (gamma)
  motiv ~~ motiv      # variance of the exogenous predictor (phi11)
'
fit_lavaan <- sem(m1, data = dat)
parameterEstimates(fit_lavaan)[, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est", "pvalue")]
```


**Interpretation:**

- Both methods estimate the slope as 0.530; higher motivation is associated with higher reading scores.
- Intercept = 0 because the variables are centered.
- Residual variance: OLS 72.05 vs. ML 71.77; predictor variance in lavaan = 99.80. The difference comes from the denominators used in estimation.
- df = 0: three covariance moments and three parameters (excluding means). Global fit is not testable.

## Multiple regression

```{r}
#| label: m2
m2 <- '
  read ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv   # two gammas plus the intercept
  ppsych ~~ motiv             # covariance between the predictors (phi21)
'
fit2 <- sem(m2, data = dat)
brief(fit2)
```

**Interpretation:** Reading is predicted by motivation (+0.461) and negative parental psychology (−0.275). Predictor covariance = −24.95; reading residual variance = 64.71. The model is saturated.

## Multivariate regression

```{r}
#| label: m3a
m3a <- '
  read  ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv
  arith ~ 1 + motiv            # ppsych -> arith is fixed to 0 by leaving it out
'
fit3a <- sem(m3a, data = dat)
brief(fit3a)
```

```{r}
#| label: m3d
m3d <- '
  read  ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv
  arith ~ 1 + motiv
  read ~~ 0*arith       # force the residual covariance to zero
'
fit3d <- sem(m3d, data = dat)
brief(fit3d)
```

```{r}
#| label: m3e
m3e <- '
  read  ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv
  arith ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv   # every predictor on every outcome
'
fit3e <- sem(m3e, data = dat)
brief(fit3e)
```

| Model | Outcomes | Predictors | Regression paths | Residual covariance | Covariance-model parameters* | df |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 2 | read | ppsych, motiv | 2 | Not applicable | 6 | 0 |
| 3A | read, arith | ppsych, motiv | 3 | Free | 9 | 1 |
| 3D | read, arith | ppsych, motiv | 3 | Fixed to zero | 8 | 2 |
| 3E | read, arith | ppsych, motiv | 4 | Free | 10 | 0 |

*Counts exclude means and include predictor variances/covariance. Each outcome has a residual variance. lavaan's reported count can differ when predictors are fixed.

**Key difference:** Multiple regression has one outcome; multivariate regression has several. Model 3D fits poorly because it removes the shared residual variation of reading and arithmetic. Model 3E is saturated.

## Path analysis

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  P[Parental psychology] --> R[Reading]
  M[Motivation] --> R
  M --> A[Arithmetic]
  R --> A
  P <--> M
```

```{r}
#| label: m4a
m4a <- '
  read  ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv
  arith ~ 1 + motiv + read     # read predicts arith: a beta path
'
fit4a <- sem(m4a, data = dat)
brief(fit4a)
```


- Parental psychology → reading: −0.275.
- Motivation → reading: 0.461.
- Motivation → arithmetic: 0.296.
- Reading → arithmetic: 0.573.
- Motivation also has an indirect relationship with arithmetic through reading (0.461 × 0.573 ≈ 0.264).

# Model Fit

```{r}
#| label: fit4a-measures
fitMeasures(fit4a, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli",
                     "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr",
                     "baseline.chisq", "baseline.df"))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Output: M4c baseline
```{r}
#| label: m4c-baseline
m4c <- '
  read   ~~ read
  arith  ~~ arith
  ppsych ~~ ppsych
  motiv  ~~ motiv
'
fit4c <- sem(m4c, data = dat)
fitMeasures(fit4c, c("chisq", "df"))
```
:::

| Measure | Meaning | Model 4A |
|---|---|---|
| Chi-square | Tests exact fit | 4.87, p = .027 |
| df | Available model restrictions | 1 |
| CFI | Improvement over baseline | .994 |
| TLI | Improvement adjusted for complexity | .971 |
| RMSEA | Approximate misfit per df | .088 |
| SRMR | Average standardized residual discrepancy | .015 |

**Interpretation:** CFI, TLI and SRMR look good, but chi-square rejects exact fit. RMSEA is uncertain with only one df. Overall fit is reasonably close, with some misfit. The baseline model represents minimal relationships; lavaan retains fixed exogenous covariances where appropriate.

## Model identification

**df = known moments − free parameters.**

- Saturated: reproduces observed moments exactly.
- Just-identified: df = 0, unique solution if identified; no global fit test.
- Over-identified: df > 0; fit can be assessed if identified.
- Under-identified: too few independent moments or constraints for a unique solution (negative df is one warning).


```{r}
#| label: m4b
# Model 4B: add ppsych -> arith, which uses up the last df
m4b <- '
  read  ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv
  arith ~ 1 + ppsych + motiv + read
'
fit4b <- sem(m4b, data = dat)
fitMeasures(fit4b, c("chisq", "df"))

# Likelihood-ratio test of the one restriction in 4A
anova(fit4b, fit4a)
```

Adding the direct parental psychology → arithmetic path uses the remaining df. Model 4B is saturated.

# Modification Indices

```{r}
#| label: mi-4a
head(modindices(fit4a, sort = TRUE), 5)
```

- **MI:** expected chi-square reduction when one fixed parameter is freed (one df for a single independent restriction).
- **EPC:** expected value of the newly freed parameter.
- The MI for `arith ~ ppsych` is about 4.85, close to the actual chi-square reduction of 4.87.
- A large MI does not mean a path is theoretically valid. Adding paths just to improve fit can cause overfitting and poor replication.

# Measurement Model

```{r}
#| label: m5a
# Model 5A: one factor, three indicators (the seminar's Risk example)
m5a <- '
  risk =~ verbal + ses + ppsych
'
fit5a <- cfa(m5a, data = dat)
brief(fit5a)
```

```{r}
#| label: measurement
measurement_model <- '
  adjust  =~ motiv + harm + stabi      # Adjustment
  risk    =~ ppsych + ses + verbal     # Risk
  achieve =~ read + arith + spell      # Achievement
'
fit_measurement <- cfa(
  measurement_model,
  data = dat
)
brief(fit_measurement)
```


The single-factor model with three indicators is just-identified under the usual constraints. The three-factor CFA has 45 covariance moments and 21 parameters, giving 24 df.

| Factor | Standardized loadings (indicator order above) |
|---|---|
| Adjustment | .93, .83, .65 |
| Risk | .56, −.59, −.73 |
| Achievement | .94, .79, .92 |

**Interpretation:** Achievement has the strongest indicators. Risk is less consistently measured. Residual variances represent indicator variance not explained by the factor. Negative Risk loadings reflect the marker direction.

**Fit:** CFI = .951, TLI = .927, RMSEA = .102, SRMR = .041. Mixed results; RMSEA indicates notable misfit despite the favorable SRMR.


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Output: Mi measurement
```{r}
#| label: mi-measurement
head(modindices(fit_measurement, sort = TRUE), 5)
```
:::

# Structural Regression Model

## Model 6A: One endogenous factor

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A((Adjustment)) --> C((Achievement))
  B((Risk)) --> C
  A <--> B
```


```{r}
#| label: structural
structural_model <- '
  # Measurement model
  adjust  =~ motiv + harm + stabi
  risk    =~ ppsych + ses + verbal
  achieve =~ read + arith + spell

  # Structural model
  achieve ~ adjust + risk
'
fit_structural <- sem(
  structural_model,
  data = dat
)
brief(fit_structural)
```


- Adjustment → Achievement: standardized .37 (positive).
- Risk → Achievement: standardized −.56 (negative and stronger in magnitude).
- Adjustment and Risk correlate −.47.
- Achievement R² = .653; about 65% of variance is explained, leaving about 35% unexplained.
- Fit is identical to CFA because the latent structural part is saturated. Overall fit remains mixed.

## Model 6B: Two endogenous factors

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  R((Risk)) --> A((Adjustment))
  R --> C((Achievement))
  A --> C
```

```{r}
#| label: m6b
m6b <- '
  # Measurement model
  adjust  =~ motiv + harm + stabi
  risk    =~ ppsych + ses + verbal
  achieve =~ read + arith + spell

  # Structural model (labels a, b, c name the paths)
  adjust  ~ a*risk               # gamma11
  achieve ~ b*adjust + c*risk    # beta21 and gamma21

  # Defined parameters
  indirect := a*b                # Risk -> Adjustment -> Achievement
  total    := c + a*b            # direct + indirect
'
fit6b <- sem(m6b, data = dat)
brief(fit6b)
```


| Effect | Standardized estimate |
|---|---:|
| Risk → Adjustment (a) | −.47 |
| Adjustment → Achievement (b) | .37 |
| Risk → Achievement (c) | −.56 |
| Indirect (a × b) | −.18 |
| Total (c + a × b) | −.74 |

**Γ** contains Risk → Adjustment and Risk → Achievement. **B** contains Adjustment → Achievement. Risk has a direct and possible indirect relationship with Achievement. Identical fit does not establish causal direction.

**Marker note:** UCLA uses verbal IQ first for Risk in Model 6A; this note uses parental psychology first. The sign and scale change, but fit does not.


# Practice Questions and Answers

| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| 1. What is structural equation modeling? | SEM combines measurement and regression models to examine relationships among variables. |
| 2. Which statistical models can be treated as special cases of SEM? | Simple, multiple and multivariate regression, path analysis, CFA and structural regression. |
| 3. What is the difference between an observed variable and a latent variable? | Observed variables are measured directly; latent variables are inferred from indicators. |
| 4. What is the difference between an exogenous variable and an endogenous variable? | Exogenous variables are not predicted within the model; endogenous variables are. |
| 5. What is the difference between a measurement model and a structural model? | Measurement links factors to indicators; structural models link variables to one another. |
| 6. What does the `~` operator mean in lavaan? | `~` means is regressed on. |
| 7. What does the `=~` operator mean? | `=~` means is measured by. |
| 8. What does the `~~` operator mean? | `~~` specifies variance or covariance, including residual covariance. |
| 9. What is the difference between a regression path and a factor loading? | A loading links a factor to an indicator; a regression path links model variables. |
| 10. What is the difference between a sample covariance matrix and a model-implied covariance matrix? | S comes from the data; Σ(θ) comes from the model. |
| 11. Why does `cov()` produce a sample covariance matrix rather than a population covariance matrix? | `cov()` uses sample observations and divides by n − 1. |
| 12. What is the difference between multiple regression and multivariate regression? | Multiple regression has several predictors and one outcome; multivariate regression has several outcomes. |
| 13. Why are some models saturated? | They freely reproduce all relevant observed moments. |
| 14. What does it mean when a model has zero degrees of freedom? | There is no remaining df for a global fit test. |
| 15. What does it mean when a model has negative degrees of freedom? | There are more free parameters than available moments, so the model is under-identified. |
| 16. What is the difference between the Γ and B matrices? | Γ links exogenous to endogenous variables; B links endogenous variables to one another. |
| 17. What is a modification index? | MI estimates the chi-square improvement from freeing one parameter. |
| 18. Why should researchers not automatically follow modification-index recommendations? | A suggested relationship may lack theory and overfit the sample. |
| 19. What is the difference between a direct effect and an indirect effect? | A direct effect uses one path; an indirect effect is the product of paths through a mediator. |
| 20. Which paths in the structural model are theoretically most important? | Risk → Achievement, Adjustment → Achievement, and Risk → Adjustment in Model 6B. |
| 21. How should the fit of the measurement model be evaluated? | Check loadings, residuals, chi-square, CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR together. |
| 22. How should the fit of the structural model be evaluated? | Review fit and structural paths, and compare with CFA or restricted models. |
| 23. What conclusions can be drawn from the standardized estimates? | Standardized estimates allow comparison of relative path strengths; Risk has the larger association with Achievement. |
| 24. What limitations should be considered when interpreting this SEM? | Cross-sectional data cannot establish causation; measurement misfit, marker choice and equivalent models limit interpretation. |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Additional UCLA concept checks


**Does `cov(dat)` give the population covariance matrix Σ?** No. It gives the sample covariance matrix S, an estimate of Σ from our 500 students.

**Σ(θ) is the covariance matrix reproduced from the model parameters. True or false?** True. It's what the model implies the covariances should be.

**If an observed variable is predicted by an endogenous factor, is it an x-side indicator?** False. Indicators of an endogenous factor (η) are y-side indicators. Whether an indicator is x or y depends on its factor, not on the fact that it's predicted.

**In Model 1A, what do the estimates correspond to in the diagram, and why is the motiv intercept zero?** γ₁ = 0.53, α = 0, ψ₁₁ = 71.77. The intercept is zero because the variables are centered. The exogenous variance φ₁₁ isn't printed by default but can be requested with `motiv ~~ motiv`.

**What happens if you drop `1 +` from the regression?** The mean structure may be omitted if not otherwise requested; df remains zero here.

**Why does the simple regression have zero df?** Three knowns (two variances, one covariance) and three parameters (γ₁, φ₁₁, ψ₁₁): 3 − 3 = 0.

**Why does `m1b` show 5 free parameters?** The four listed parameters plus the intercept of `motiv`, which lavaan adds implicitly when the mean structure is on.

**`lm()` uses least squares and lavaan uses maximum likelihood. True or false?** True. The slopes match, but the residual variances differ slightly because ML divides by *n* instead of *n* − 2.

**In Model 2, can α be written as α₁ as in Model 1A?** With one outcome, α is just that outcome's intercept. In multivariate models each outcome gets its own intercept (α₁, α₂).

**Re-run Model 2 without `ppsych ~~ motiv`. What changes?** The coefficients don't change and df stays 0. Only the parameter count reported changes, because lavaan fixes the predictor covariance at its sample value instead of listing it.

**Γ is always square. True or false?** False. Γ has one row per endogenous variable and one column per exogenous variable. In Model 3A it's 2 × 2 only by coincidence.

**γ₁₂ is the coefficient of x₂ on y₁. True or false?** True. Subscripts are read "to, from".

**Multivariate regression in lavaan is the same as running separate regressions. True or false?** False by default, because `sem()` covaries the residuals. Fix the covariance to zero (Model 3D) and the coefficients match the separate regressions.

**In Model 3D, is `.arith` the variance of arithmetic?** No. The dot means residual variance: what's left of arithmetic after motivation.

**How many free parameters and df does Model 3A have?** 10 knowns, 9 free parameters (γ₂₁ is fixed to 0), so df = 1.

**Over-identified models are good because fit can be assessed. True or false?** True, if the model is identified; positive df permits a global fit test.

**β₂₁ equals β₁₂. True or false?** False. β₂₁ is the path from y₁ to y₂ (read → arith); β₁₂ would be the reverse, and in Model 4A it's fixed to zero.

**Which single path separates Model 3A from Model 4A?** `read → arith`. Model 4A replaces the residual covariance with a directional path from reading to arithmetic.

**The diagonal of B is always zero. True or false?** True. A variable can't predict itself.

**B = 0 corresponds to multivariate regression. True or false?** True. With no paths among the endogenous variables, all that's left is Γ, which is multivariate regression.

**You should always use modification indices to improve fit. True or false?** False. They are diagnostics, not instructions.

**Each modification index tests one parameter at a time. True or false?** True. That's why each is a 1-df chi-square.

**Re-run Model 4B and compare with the MI. Do they match?** The coefficient matches the EPC exactly (0.068), and the chi-square drop (4.870) is close to the MI (4.847). The MI is an approximation.

**Why does `fit4b` have no modification indices left?** It is saturated; there is no remaining global misfit to resolve.

**Residual covariance is Σ − Σ(θ), and closer to zero is better. True or false?** False as written. We never see Σ, so the residual covariance is S − Σ(θ̂). Closer to zero is better.

**A larger chi-square means larger residual covariances. True or false?** Not necessarily for every individual residual; chi-square measures overall weighted discrepancy.

**A CFA has 20 df. Under the χ²/df < 2 rule, what chi-square is acceptable?** Below 40 under that heuristic.

**x-indicators have no residual terms. True or false?** False. Every indicator has a residual (δ for x-side, ε for y-side) and a residual variance.

**Is a one-factor model with three indicators just-, over- or under-identified?** Just-identified. Six knowns, six parameters, df = 0 (Model 5A).

**In Model 6A, B = 0 means there are no structural paths. True or false?** False. B = 0 only means no paths among endogenous latent variables. The structural paths are in Γ.

**In Model 6A, η has one element and Γ is 1 × 2. True or false?** True. One endogenous factor (Achievement) and two exogenous factors.

**What extra matrix is needed when one exogenous factor predicts two endogenous factors and one of those predicts the other?** B. Model 6B puts Adjustment → Achievement in B.

**Multivariate regression always has more than one exogenous predictor. True or false?** False. Multivariate means more than one outcome. It can have a single predictor.
:::

# Key Takeaways and Reflection

- SEM brings regression, path analysis and CFA together.
- Model identification matters before interpreting fit.
- Fit measures should be read together, not individually.
- Modification indices are diagnostic tools, not instructions.

My main takeaway was how CFA connects to SEM. I can use this in marketing research to study brand trust and purchase intention without assuming causation.
